name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_ASSERTION_REASON_Q01 - Atomic radius anomaly of gallium and aluminium

questiontext.text:
Assertion (A): The atomic radius of gallium (\(135\text{ pm}\)) is smaller than that of aluminium (\(143\text{ pm}\)).

Reason (R): Gallium contains \(10\) inner \(d\)-electrons which offer poor shielding effect for the outer electrons against the increased nuclear charge.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Atomic radius generally increases down a group as a new electron shell is added. However, the effective nuclear charge experienced by valence electrons depends on the shielding (screening) efficiency of inner-core electrons, which follows the order \(s > p > d > f\).

Step 2: Evaluation of the Assertion
Moving from aluminium (\(\text{Al}\), atomic number \(13\), electronic configuration \([\text{Ne}]3s^2 3p^1\)) to gallium (\(\text{Ga}\), atomic number \(31\), electronic configuration \([\text{Ar}]3d^{10} 4s^2 4p^1\)), the atomic radius decreases from \(143\text{ pm}\) to \(135\text{ pm}\). Thus, the assertion is correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Reason
Unlike aluminium, which has a noble gas inner core, gallium has \(10\) additional \(3d\)-electrons in its inner core. Because \(d\)-orbitals are diffuse, these \(10\) \(d\)-electrons provide poor shielding against the increased nuclear charge, pulling the outer \(4s\) and \(4p\) electrons closer to the nucleus. Thus, the reason is correct.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Both the assertion and the reason are correct, and the poor shielding effect of the \(10\) inner \(d\)-electrons directly explains why gallium has a smaller atomic radius than aluminium.

answer.text: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A).
(A) is correct but (R) is incorrect.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_ASSERTION_REASON_Q02 - Acidic nature of orthoboric acid in water

questiontext.text:
Assertion (A): Orthoboric acid (\(\mathrm{H_3BO_3}\)) behaves as a weak monobasic Lewis acid in aqueous solution.

Reason (R): Orthoboric acid dissociates directly in water by donating a proton (\(\mathrm{H^+}\)) from its \(-\mathrm{OH}\) group.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A protonic (Brønsted-Lowry) acid donates \(\mathrm{H^+}\) ions directly from its own molecule, whereas a Lewis acid accepts an electron pair to complete its valence shell.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Assertion
In \(\mathrm{B(OH)_3}\), the boron atom has only six electrons in its valence shell and is electron-deficient. In water, it acts as a weak monobasic Lewis acid by accepting a hydroxyl ion (\(\mathrm{OH^-}\)) from a water molecule: \(\mathrm{B(OH)_3 + 2H_2O \rightarrow [B(OH)_4]^- + H_3O^+}\). Thus, the assertion is correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Reason
Orthoboric acid is not a protonic acid because it cannot release \(\mathrm{H^+}\) ions on its own; instead, it accepts \(\mathrm{OH^-}\) from water, which in turn releases \(\mathrm{H_3O^+}\) ions. Thus, the reason is incorrect.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The assertion is correct, whereas the reason is incorrect.

answer.text: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_ASSERTION_REASON_Q03 - Maximum covalence of boron in fluoro complexes

questiontext.text:
Assertion (A): Boron forms \([\mathrm{BF_4}]^-\) ion, whereas it is unable to form \([\mathrm{BF_6}]^{3-}\) ion.

Reason (R): Boron belongs to the second period and lacks \(d\)-orbitals in its valence shell, restricting its maximum covalence to \(4\).

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The maximum covalence of an element is determined by the number of available valence orbitals that can participate in bond formation.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Assertion
Boron readily accepts a fluoride ion in \(\mathrm{BF_3}\) to form the tetrahedral \([\mathrm{BF_4}]^-\) ion, but it never forms the octahedral \([\mathrm{BF_6}]^{3-}\) ion (unlike aluminium, which forms \([\mathrm{AlF_6}]^{3-}\)). Thus, the assertion is correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Reason
Boron has the electronic configuration \(1s^2 2s^2 2p^1\). In its valence shell (\(n=2\)), only one \(2s\) and three \(2p\) orbitals are available, and \(2d\)-orbitals do not exist. Therefore, boron can accommodate at most four electron pairs, limiting its maximum covalence to \(4\). Thus, the reason is correct.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Both the assertion and the reason are correct, and the absence of \(d\)-orbitals in the second-period element boron directly explains why it forms \([\mathrm{BF_4}]^-\) but cannot expand its octet to form \([\mathrm{BF_6}]^{3-}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_ASSERTION_REASON_Q04 - Oxidation state stability in thallium and boron

questiontext.text:
Assertion (A): In thallium, the \(+1\) oxidation state is predominant and more stable than the \(+3\) oxidation state.

Reason (R): The sum of the first three ionisation enthalpies of boron is very high due to its small atomic size.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In Group \(13\), the relative stability of the \(+1\) oxidation state increases down the group (\(\text{Al} < \text{Ga} < \text{In} < \text{Tl}\)) due to the inert pair effect, where poor shielding by intervening \(d\) and \(f\) orbitals causes the \(ns^2\) electrons to be held tightly.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Assertion
For thallium (\([\text{Xe}]4f^{14} 5d^{10} 6s^2 6p^1\)), the \(6s^2\) electrons are strongly attracted to the nucleus due to poor shielding by the \(4f\) and \(5d\) electrons. Consequently, only the \(6p^1\) electron participates readily in bonding, making the \(+1\) oxidation state predominant and more stable than the \(+3\) oxidation state (which is strongly oxidising). Thus, the assertion is correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Reason
Because boron has a very small atomic size, the sum of its first three ionisation enthalpies (\(\Delta_i H_1 + \Delta_i H_2 + \Delta_i H_3 = 801 + 2427 + 3659 = 6887\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)) is very high, preventing it from forming \(\mathrm{B^{3+}}\) ions and forcing it to form covalent compounds. Thus, the reason is also a correct statement.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Both the assertion and the reason are correct statements, but the high sum of ionisation enthalpies of boron does not explain the predominance of the \(+1\) oxidation state in thallium (which is caused by the inert pair effect).

answer.text: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_ASSERTION_REASON_Q05 - Passivity of aluminium with concentrated nitric acid

questiontext.text:
Assertion (A): Concentrated nitric acid reacts vigorously with aluminium to liberate dihydrogen gas.

Reason (R): Concentrated nitric acid renders aluminium passive by forming a protective oxide layer on its surface.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Although aluminium is an amphoteric metal that dissolves in dilute mineral acids (such as dilute \(\mathrm{HCl}\)) with the liberation of \(\mathrm{H_2}\) gas, its behaviour with strong oxidising acids like concentrated \(\mathrm{HNO_3}\) is governed by surface passivation.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Assertion
Aluminium does not react vigorously with concentrated nitric acid to liberate dihydrogen gas; in fact, concentrated \(\mathrm{HNO_3}\) can be transported in aluminium containers because no sustained reaction occurs. Thus, the assertion is incorrect.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Reason
Concentrated nitric acid is a strong oxidising agent that forms a very thin, protective layer of aluminium oxide (\(\mathrm{Al_2O_3}\)) on the surface of aluminium, rendering the metal passive toward further attack. Thus, the reason is correct.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The assertion is incorrect, whereas the reason is correct.

answer.text: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_ASSERTION_REASON_Q06 - Terminal and bridging bonds in diborane

questiontext.text:
Assertion (A): In diborane (\(\mathrm{B_2H_6}\)), the two bridging \(\mathrm{B-H-B}\) bonds are longer (\(134\text{ pm}\)) and weaker than the four terminal \(\mathrm{B-H}\) bonds (\(119\text{ pm}\)).

Reason (R): The four terminal \(\mathrm{B-H}\) bonds are normal two-centre two-electron (\(2c\text{-}2e\)) bonds, whereas the two bridging \(\mathrm{B-H-B}\) bonds are three-centre two-electron (\(3c\text{-}2e\)) bonds.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In electron-deficient molecules such as diborane (\(\mathrm{B_2H_6}\)), each boron atom is \(sp^3\) hybridised with four hybrid orbitals but only three valence electrons, requiring multicentre bonding to link the two \(\mathrm{BH_2}\) units.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Assertion
Experimental structural data for diborane show that the four terminal \(\mathrm{B-H}\) bonds lying in one plane have a bond length of \(119\text{ pm}\), whereas the two bridging \(\mathrm{B-H}\) bonds above and below the plane have a longer bond length of \(134\text{ pm}\) and are weaker. Thus, the assertion is correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Reason
Each terminal \(\mathrm{B-H}\) bond is formed by the overlap of a half-filled \(sp^3\) orbital of boron and a \(1s\) orbital of hydrogen, constituting a regular \(2c\text{-}2e\) bond. Each bridging \(\mathrm{B-H-B}\) bond (banana bond) involves the overlap of one \(sp^3\) orbital from each of the two boron atoms (one containing an electron, one empty) with the \(1s\) orbital of a single hydrogen atom, sharing two electrons across three centres (\(3c\text{-}2e\)). Thus, the reason is correct.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Both the assertion and the reason are correct, and because only two electrons are shared among three nuclei in each \(3c\text{-}2e\) bridge bond, the electron density between \(\mathrm{B}\) and \(\mathrm{H}\) is lower than in a \(2c\text{-}2e\) terminal bond, making the bridge bonds longer and weaker. Hence, the reason correctly explains the assertion.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_ASSERTION_REASON_Q07 - Hydrolysis of carbon and silicon tetrachlorides

questiontext.text:
Assertion (A): Carbon tetrachloride (\(\mathrm{CCl_4}\)) is not hydrolysed by water, whereas silicon tetrachloride (\(\mathrm{SiCl_4}\)) is easily hydrolysed to form silicic acid.

Reason (R): Carbon is more electronegative than silicon and cannot accept a lone pair of electrons from water even though carbon has vacant \(d\)-orbitals in its valence shell.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Hydrolysis of Group \(14\) tetrachlorides (\(\mathrm{MCl_4}\)) proceeds by nucleophilic attack of a water molecule, where the central atom accepts a lone pair of electrons from oxygen into a vacant low-energy orbital.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Assertion
\(\mathrm{CCl_4}\) resists hydrolysis in water, whereas \(\mathrm{SiCl_4}\) undergoes rapid hydrolysis with water to yield silicic acid, \(\mathrm{Si(OH)_4}\), and \(\mathrm{HCl}\). Thus, the assertion is correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Reason
Carbon is a second-period element (\(1s^2 2s^2 2p^2\)) and does not have vacant \(d\)-orbitals in its valence shell. In contrast, silicon (\(3s^2 3p^2\)) possesses vacant \(3d\)-orbitals capable of accepting the lone pair of electrons from water. Claiming that carbon has vacant \(d\)-orbitals makes the reason incorrect.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The assertion is correct, whereas the reason is incorrect.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_ASSERTION_REASON_Q08 - Properties and stability of graphite and diamond

questiontext.text:
Assertion (A): Graphite is soft, slippery, and conducts electricity along its layers, whereas diamond is extremely hard and an electrical insulator.

Reason (R): Graphite is thermodynamically the most stable allotrope of carbon with standard enthalpy of formation \(\Delta_f H^\circ = 0\).

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The physical properties of carbon allotropes depend on their crystal lattice and hybridisation state, whereas thermodynamic stability is reflected in their standard enthalpy of formation (\(\Delta_f H^\circ\)).

Step 2: Evaluation of the Assertion
In graphite, each carbon is \(sp^2\) hybridised, forming planar hexagonal sheets held together by weak van der Waals forces (\(340\text{ pm}\) apart), allowing layers to slide (soft and slippery), while the fourth delocalised \(\pi\)-electron conducts electricity along the sheet. In diamond, each carbon is \(sp^3\) hybridised in a rigid three-dimensional network with all valence electrons localised in strong covalent bonds, making it extremely hard and non-conducting. Thus, the assertion is correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Reason
Graphite is indeed thermodynamically the most stable allotrope of carbon, so its standard enthalpy of formation \(\Delta_f H^\circ\) is taken as \(0\) (compared to \(1.90\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\) for diamond and \(38.1\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\) for \(\mathrm{C_{60}}\)). Thus, the reason is correct.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Both the assertion and the reason are correct statements, but thermodynamic stability (\(\Delta_f H^\circ = 0\)) does not explain the differences in hardness, lubricity, and electrical conductivity between graphite and diamond (which arise from their \(sp^2\) layered versus \(sp^3\) 3D-network structures).

questiontext.text:
Assertion (A): Lead forms stable \(\mathrm{PbI_2}\), whereas \(\mathrm{PbI_4}\) does not exist.

Reason (R): The \(\mathrm{Pb-I}\) bond initially formed during the reaction does not release sufficient energy to unpair the \(6s^2\) electrons and excite one of them to a higher orbital to provide four unpaired electrons around lead.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
For a Group \(14\) element with valence configuration \(ns^2 np^2\) to exhibit tetravalency (\(\mathrm{MX_4}\)), one \(ns\) electron must be promoted to a vacant \(np\) orbital, which requires promotion energy compensated by the formation of two additional \(\mathrm{M-X}\) bonds.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Assertion
In lead, the \(+2\) oxidation state is much more stable than the \(+4\) oxidation state due to the inert pair effect, and \(\mathrm{PbI_2}\) is stable whereas \(\mathrm{PbI_4}\) does not exist. Thus, the assertion is correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Reason
The \(\mathrm{Pb-I}\) bond is relatively weak, so the energy released upon forming \(\mathrm{Pb-I}\) bonds is insufficient to unpair the tightly held \(6s^2\) electrons and promote one electron to a \(6p\) orbital to achieve four unpaired electrons. (Additionally, \(\mathrm{I^-}\) is a strong reducing agent and \(\mathrm{Pb^{4+}}\) is a strong oxidising agent.) Thus, the reason is correct.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Both the assertion and the reason are correct, and the insufficient energy released by \(\mathrm{Pb-I}\) bond formation to unpair and excite the \(6s^2\) electrons directly explains why \(\mathrm{PbI_4}\) does not exist while \(\mathrm{PbI_2}\) is stable.

questiontext.text:
Assertion (A): Silicon readily forms both \([\mathrm{SiF_6}]^{2-}\) and \([\mathrm{SiCl_6}]^{2-}\) octahedral complex ions.

Reason (R): Six large chloride ions cannot be accommodated around the small \(\mathrm{Si^{4+}}\) ion, and the interaction between the lone pair of a chloride ion and \(\mathrm{Si^{4+}}\) is not very strong.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The formation of six-coordinated \(sp^3d^2\) complexes of silicon depends not only on the availability of vacant \(3d\)-orbitals, but also on steric factors (size of ligands relative to \(\mathrm{Si^{4+}}\)) and the strength of the coordinate bond formed.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Assertion
While \([\mathrm{SiF_6}]^{2-}\) is well known and stable, \([\mathrm{SiCl_6}]^{2-}\) is not known to exist. Therefore, the assertion is incorrect.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Reason
Two factors prevent the formation of \([\mathrm{SiCl_6}]^{2-}\): first, six bulky \(\mathrm{Cl^-}\) ions cannot be packed around the small \(\mathrm{Si^{4+}}\) ion due to steric crowding; second, the interaction between the lone pair of \(\mathrm{Cl^-}\) and \(\mathrm{Si^{4+}}\) is not strong enough to stabilise the \(6\)-coordinated species. Thus, the reason is correct.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The assertion is incorrect, whereas the reason is correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_ASSERTION_REASON_Q11 - Chemical reactivity of silica and hydrophobicity of silicones

questiontext.text:
Assertion (A): Silicon dioxide (\(\mathrm{SiO_2}\)) resists attack by halogens, dihydrogen, and most acids even at elevated temperatures, but is attacked by \(\mathrm{HF}\) and \(\mathrm{NaOH}\).

Reason (R): Silicones are water-repelling in nature because the \(\mathrm{Si-O}\) polymer chain is surrounded by non-polar alkyl or aryl groups.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Silica (\(\mathrm{SiO_2}\)) is a three-dimensional covalent network solid with very high \(\mathrm{Si-O}\) bond enthalpy, whereas silicones are organosilicon polymers containing \((\mathrm{R_2SiO})\) repeating units.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Assertion
Due to its high \(\mathrm{Si-O}\) bond enthalpy and giant network structure, \(\mathrm{SiO_2}\) is almost non-reactive toward halogens, \(\mathrm{H_2}\), and most acids and metals. However, it reacts with \(\mathrm{HF}\) (\(\mathrm{SiO_2 + 4HF \rightarrow SiF_4 + 2H_2O}\)) and \(\mathrm{NaOH}\) (\(\mathrm{SiO_2 + 2NaOH \rightarrow Na_2SiO_3 + H_2O}\)). Thus, the assertion is correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Reason
In silicones, the inorganic siloxane backbone (\(\mathrm{-Si-O-Si-}\)) is surrounded by hydrophobic, non-polar alkyl or aryl groups (\(\mathrm{R}\)), which makes silicones water-repelling. Thus, the reason is also correct.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Both the assertion and the reason are correct statements, but the hydrophobicity of silicones does not explain the selective reactivity of \(\mathrm{SiO_2}\) toward \(\mathrm{HF}\) and \(\mathrm{NaOH}\).
